topic: 20-day deadline to file a Defence in Ontario Small Claims Court
summary: If you are served with a Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) in Ontario Small Claims Court, you have 20 days to file a Defence (Form 9A) with the court. Filing on time is what stops you from losing automatically.
officialCitation: Rules of the Small Claims Court, O. Reg. 258/98, r. 9.01
sourceTitle: O. Reg. 258/98 — Rules of the Small Claims Court (Rule 9, Defence)

topic: What happens if you miss the deadline: default judgment (Ontario)
summary: If you do not file a Defence within 20 days, the plaintiff can note you in default and ask the court for a default judgment — you lose without the merits ever being heard, which can lead to wage garnishment.
officialCitation: Rules of the Small Claims Court, O. Reg. 258/98, r. 11 (default proceedings)
sourceTitle: O. Reg. 258/98 — Rules of the Small Claims Court (Rule 11)

topic: Time-barred defence: Ontario's 2-year basic limitation period
summary: In Ontario, a proceeding generally cannot be started more than 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. For most debts that means roughly 2 years after the last payment or written acknowledgment. If the claim was started too late, raising the limitation as a defence can get the case dismissed.
officialCitation: Limitations Act, 2002, S.O. 2002, c. 24, Sched. B, ss. 4 & 5
sourceTitle: Limitations Act, 2002 — basic limitation period & discovery

topic: What can restart the Ontario 2-year clock: a written acknowledgment or payment
summary: A written acknowledgment of the debt, or in some cases a payment, made before the limitation period expires can restart the 2-year clock. That is why the date of your last payment or written acknowledgment matters when judging whether an Ontario debt is time-barred.
officialCitation: Limitations Act, 2002, S.O. 2002, c. 24, Sched. B, s. 13
sourceTitle: Limitations Act, 2002 — acknowledgment of liability (s. 13)

topic: Make a debt buyer prove it owns the debt (Ontario)
summary: When the plaintiff is a debt buyer rather than the original creditor, it must be able to prove it actually owns your debt and that it was properly assigned to it. You can put the plaintiff to strict proof of the assignment and the chain of ownership; gaps are a real defence.
officialCitation: Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.34, s. 53 (absolute assignment)
sourceTitle: Conveyancing and Law of Property Act — assignment of debts (s. 53)

topic: Honest path: admit what you owe and propose terms of payment (Ontario)
summary: If you genuinely owe the debt and simply need affordable terms, the Defence (Form 9A) lets you admit the claim and propose a payment schedule you can manage. Filing this still protects you from a harsh default judgment.
officialCitation: Rules of the Small Claims Court, O. Reg. 258/98, Form 9A (Defence — proposal of terms of payment)
sourceTitle: O. Reg. 258/98 — Defence (Form 9A), proposal of terms

topic: The Defence (Form 9A) — Ontario
summary: Form 9A is the official Defence used to respond to a Plaintiff's Claim in Ontario Small Claims Court. It is where you say what you admit or deny, raise any defences (such as the limitation period), and, if you admit the debt, propose terms of payment.
officialCitation: Rules of the Small Claims Court, O. Reg. 258/98, Form 9A
sourceTitle: Ontario Court Services — Small Claims Court Forms (Form 9A, Defence)

topic: 14-day deadline to file a Reply in BC Small Claims
summary: If you are served in British Columbia with a Notice of Claim in Provincial Court Small Claims, you have 14 days to file a Reply (Form 2) — 30 days if you were served outside BC. Filing on time is what stops you from losing automatically.
officialCitation: Small Claims Rules, B.C. Reg. 261/93, r. 3 (reply within 14 days)
sourceTitle: B.C. Reg. 261/93 — Small Claims Rules (Rule 3, Reply)

topic: What happens if you miss the deadline: default order (BC)
summary: If you do not file a Reply within the time allowed, the registrar can make a default order against you — you lose without the merits being heard, which can lead to enforcement against your wages or assets.
officialCitation: Small Claims Rules, B.C. Reg. 261/93, r. 3 (default order where no reply filed)
sourceTitle: B.C. Reg. 261/93 — Small Claims Rules (Rule 3)

topic: Time-barred defence: BC's 2-year basic limitation period
summary: British Columbia has a single 2-year basic limitation period — a court proceeding generally cannot be started more than 2 years after the claim was discovered. For most debts that is roughly 2 years after the last payment or written acknowledgment.
officialCitation: Limitation Act, S.B.C. 2012, c. 13, s. 6 (basic limitation period)
sourceTitle: Limitation Act (BC) — basic limitation period (s. 6)

topic: What can restart the BC 2-year clock: a written acknowledgment or payment
summary: An acknowledgment of liability for a debt — in writing, or by making a payment — made before the limitation period expires can restart BC's 2-year clock. The date of your last payment or written acknowledgment is what matters.
officialCitation: Limitation Act, S.B.C. 2012, c. 13, s. 24 (effect of acknowledgment)
sourceTitle: Limitation Act (BC) — acknowledgment (s. 24)

topic: Make a debt buyer prove it owns the debt (BC)
summary: When the plaintiff is a debt buyer, BC's Law and Equity Act requires an assignment to be absolute, in writing, and with written notice to you before the assignee can enforce it. Put the plaintiff to strict proof of the assignment and the chain of ownership.
officialCitation: Law and Equity Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 253, s. 36 (absolute assignment of a debt)
sourceTitle: Law and Equity Act (BC) — assignment of debts (s. 36)

topic: The Reply (Form 2) — British Columbia
summary: Form 2 is the Reply used to respond to a Notice of Claim in BC Provincial Court Small Claims. It is where you say what you admit or deny, raise any defences (such as the limitation period), and, if you admit the debt, propose how you will pay.
officialCitation: Small Claims Rules, B.C. Reg. 261/93, Form 2 (Reply)
sourceTitle: B.C. Reg. 261/93 — Small Claims Rules (Form 2, Reply)

topic: 30-day deadline to respond to a California complaint
summary: If you are served with a summons and complaint in California, you have 30 days to file a written response (an Answer) with the court. Filing on time is what stops you from losing automatically.
officialCitation: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 412.20(a)(3) (30 days to respond after service)
sourceTitle: California Code of Civil Procedure § 412.20

topic: What happens if you miss the deadline: default judgment (California)
summary: If you do not respond within 30 days, the plaintiff can ask the court to enter your default and then a default judgment — you lose without the merits being heard, which can lead to wage garnishment or bank levies.
officialCitation: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 585 (default judgment)
sourceTitle: California Code of Civil Procedure § 585

topic: Time-barred defence: California's 4-year limit on written-contract / credit-card debt
summary: In California, an action on a written contract must generally be filed within 4 years. Courts treat most credit-card debt as a written contract, so a credit-card lawsuit filed more than 4 years after the breach (commonly the last payment or charge-off) may be time-barred.
officialCitation: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337 (4-year limit, written contracts)
sourceTitle: California Code of Civil Procedure § 337

topic: What can restart the California clock: a new written promise
summary: In California, the limitation period can be restarted by a new promise to pay or an acknowledgment of the debt — but it must be in writing and signed. An oral promise does not restart the clock. The date of your last payment or signed acknowledgment matters.
officialCitation: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 360 (acknowledgment or new promise must be in writing)
sourceTitle: California Code of Civil Procedure § 360

topic: Make a debt buyer prove it owns the debt — California Fair Debt Buying Practices Act
summary: California's Fair Debt Buying Practices Act requires a debt buyer to actually possess proof it owns the debt before collecting or suing — the charge-off balance, the date of default, the original creditor, and documentation of the agreement. Demand it; without that proof the case can fail.
officialCitation: California Fair Debt Buying Practices Act, Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1788.50–1788.52
sourceTitle: California Civil Code — Fair Debt Buying Practices (Title 1.6C.5)

topic: The Answer (Form PLD-C-010) — California
summary: PLD-C-010 is the Judicial Council Answer—Contract form used to respond to a contract or debt complaint in California Superior Court. It is where you deny the claim, assert affirmative defences (such as the statute of limitations), and require the plaintiff to prove its case.
officialCitation: Judicial Council of California, form PLD-C-010 (Answer—Contract)
sourceTitle: California Courts — Answer—Contract (PLD-C-010)

topic: 15-day deadline to answer a court summons in Quebec
summary: If you are served with an originating application (a lawsuit) in Quebec, the summons requires you to answer it within 15 days — telling the court that you intend to defend or negotiate. Answering on time is what stops you from losing automatically.
officialCitation: Code of Civil Procedure (Québec), CQLR c. C-25.01, art. 145
sourceTitle: Code of Civil Procedure (Québec) — answer to the summons (art. 145)

topic: What happens if you miss the deadline: judgment by default (Quebec)
summary: If you do not answer the summons within 15 days, you are in default and the plaintiff can ask the court for a judgment by default — you lose without the merits being heard, which can lead to seizure of your wages or property.
officialCitation: Code of Civil Procedure (Québec), CQLR c. C-25.01, art. 180 (default to answer or defend)
sourceTitle: Code of Civil Procedure (Québec) — default (art. 180)

topic: Time-barred defence: Quebec's 3-year prescription period
summary: In Quebec, an action to enforce a personal right — which includes most debts — is prescribed (time-barred) after 3 years. For most debts that is roughly 3 years after the last payment or written acknowledgment. If the lawsuit was filed too late, raising prescription as a defence can end the case.
officialCitation: Civil Code of Québec, CQLR c. CCQ-1991, art. 2925 (three-year prescription)
sourceTitle: Civil Code of Québec — prescription of personal actions (art. 2925)

topic: What can restart the Quebec 3-year clock: acknowledging the debt
summary: Acknowledging the debt — for example by a written acknowledgment or by making a payment — interrupts prescription and restarts Quebec's 3-year clock. That is why the date of your last payment or acknowledgment matters when judging whether a Quebec debt is time-barred.
officialCitation: Civil Code of Québec, CQLR c. CCQ-1991, art. 2898 (interruption by acknowledgment)
sourceTitle: Civil Code of Québec — interruption by acknowledgment (art. 2898)

topic: Make a debt buyer prove it owns the debt (Quebec)
summary: When the plaintiff is a debt buyer rather than your original creditor, Quebec law requires a valid assignment of the claim, which can be set up against you only once you have acquiesced to it or received it. Put the plaintiff to strict proof of the assignment and that you were notified; gaps are a real defence.
officialCitation: Civil Code of Québec, CQLR c. CCQ-1991, arts. 1637 & 1641 (assignment of claims; setting up against the debtor)
sourceTitle: Civil Code of Québec — assignment of claims (arts. 1637–1641)

topic: The Answer to the summons — Quebec
summary: In Quebec you respond to a lawsuit by filing an answer to the summons — a written response stating that you intend to defend and on what basis. It is where you deny the claim and raise your defences (such as prescription), or, if you owe it, propose terms. There is no numbered form; it is a written answer filed with the court office named on the summons.
officialCitation: Code of Civil Procedure (Québec), CQLR c. C-25.01, art. 147 (content of the answer)
sourceTitle: Code of Civil Procedure (Québec) — the answer (art. 147)
